707.description: Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, delivered harsh criticism of the administration's proposed well control rule and other offshore oil and natural gas rules specifically actions taken to restrict Arctic energy production.

730.description: The Federal Lands Recreation Enhancement Act (FLREA) is set to expire at the end of September and needs to be extended to avoid losing nearly $300 million in revenues, with $180 million of that amount coming from the National Park Service (NPS) alone. This revenue is vital to the NPS for repair, maintenance, and enhancement of facilities. The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee held a hearing on FLREA this morning at which Chairman Murkowski highlighted the need for streamlining permitting  for outfitters and guides and instilling greater transparency in how fees are collected and how they’re used by the agencies. This would ensure that these fees are being used appropriately and for the maximum benefit in maintaining and improving public recreation sites.

The hearing was chaired by Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Chairman Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and EPW Subcommittee Chairman Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska.

787.title: Sen. Murkowski: These are Public Spaces, but Sure Don’t Feel Public to Us
787.description: Senator Murkowski started off Earth Day with a discussion on the reauthorization of the Land and water Conservation Act – which has for the last 50 years played a key role in creating our world-class state and federal recreation system. Murkowski highlighted the need for the reauthorization to reflect changing viewpoints about conservation in the 21st century – a switch from federal land acquisition to maintenance and enhancing accessibility. For Alaskans, a state where close to 63 percent of our lands are already held by the federal government, and where access to lands is sometimes solely by boat or plane, maintenance of facilities is a critical link between users and otherwise inaccessible lands. At a time when federal land management agencies are facing a growing maintenance backlog, access priorities need to be clearly defined. Murkowski asked about how the Interior Department identifies those priorities.

890.description: July 23, 2014 - Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, addresses Interior Secretary Sally Jewell on her complete lack of response to the community of King Cove, Alaska. 1049.title: Full Floor Speech of Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, on Izembek National Wildlife Refuge
1049.description:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski spoke on the Senate Floor regarding the Department of Interior's decision to oppose emergency road access through the Izembek National Wildlife Refuge on Alaska's Aleutian Peninsula.

Public Law 111-11, sponsored by Murkowski, orders a land exchange and construction of a road to allow the residents of King Cove access to the all-weather airport in Cold Bay for emergency evacuation purposes.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and Interior Secretary Ken Salazar on Tuesday, Feb. 5, 2013, issued a final environmental impact statement opposing the land exchange and emergency road. As required by law, Secretary Salazar still must make a public interest determination on the transfer and the road.

The land exchange, which was approved by Congress in the 2009 Izembek National Wildlife Refuge Land Exchange Act, would increase the size of the Izembek and Alaska Peninsula Wildlife Refuges by more than 56,000 acres in exchange for 206 acres of federally-owned land for the construction a single-land, gravel road to connect King Cove and Cold Bay. Use of the road would be restricted to emergencies only by law.

A dozen deaths have been attributed to the lack of road over the past 30 years. The worst accident occurred in 1981 when a plane crashed during an attempted medical evacuation, killing all four people onboard.

The law requires the Interior Secretary to determine whether the road is in the public interest -- a decision that is by law separate and distinct from the environmental impact statement. The Interior Secretary is not bound by the finding of the environmental impact statement, especially where the health and safety of a community is concerned.

30.title: Heinrich Press Conference on Republicans’ Newest Effort to Undo the Roadless Rule
30.description:
Today, June 11, 2026 at 8:30 a.m. MT / 10:30 a.m. ET, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, will host a press conference on  Republicans’ latest effort to repeal the Roadless Rule, which protects nearly 45 million acres of public lands administered by the U.S. Forest Service. U.S. Senator Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), and U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), members of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, will join Heinrich, along with Chris Wood, President and CEO of Trout Unlimited.
 
Yesterday, Republicans attached a last-minute amendment to U.S. Senator John Barrasso’s (R-Wyo.) previously bipartisan Wildfire Prevention Act to nullify the Roadless Rule. The amendment was approved on a party-line vote—11-9 —sending the amended legislation to the full Senate.
 
Last month, Heinrich joined a press conference opposing the Trump administration’s efforts to rescind the Roadless Rule and urging New Mexicans to speak out in defense of public lands. Highlighting the overwhelming public support for these protections, Heinrich noted that “99 percent of public comments supported protecting these areas.” Today we saw that every Republican on the Committee is comfortable ignoring those voices.
 
WHAT: Heinrich to Host Press Conference on Republicans’ Newest Effort to Undo the Roadless Rule, Strip Protections for Millions of Acres of Public Lands  
 
WHEN: Today, Thursday, June 11th, 2026 at 8:30 a.m. MT / 10:30 a.m. ET
 
WHO: U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
 
U.S. Senator Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
  
Chris Wood, President and CEO of Trout Unlimited, Architect of the Roadless Rule

651.title: Congressional Review Act to Repeal Steam Protection Rule-Sen. Cantwell Opposes
651.description:
February 2, 2017- Today, Ranking Member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) defended the Stream Protection Rule from being repealed via the Congressional Review Act. This rule protects communities whose water is endangered by pollution from coal mining.

Some have accused the rule of killing jobs, but the Stream Protection Rule actually protects jobs in the outdoor economy. “The outdoor economy supplies 6.1 million direct jobs in the United States. When you don’t regulate the [mining] industry and make sure they are cleaning up their mess, you are hurting the 6.1 million jobs that depend on having clean streams. The outdoor economy is just as important, is actually producing more jobs and is producing more revenue.”

Prior to today, the Congressional Review Act has only been used successfully one other time, during the George W. Bush administration. Use of the Congressional Review Act is significant because it blocks an agency from issuing any “new rule that is substantially the same” in the future without new authorizing legislation from Congress.

652.title: Protecting the Stream Protection Rule-Sen. Cantwell's Floor Remarks
652.description:
February 2, 2017- Ranking Member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) gives floor remarks on the importance of safeguarding the stream protection rule from being reversed. Repealing the Stream Protection Rule via the Congressional Review Act would threaten clean water and public health, protecting industry interests over the needs of the communities affected by mining near rivers, streams and watersheds.

The rule was released in December 2016. It established a long-overdue monitoring requirement for water pollution and prevented dewatering of streams. Toxic pollutants including lead, arsenic and selenium (known to cause birth defects and other severe human health impacts) must be monitored under the rule. This rule complements the Clean Water Act's protections that apply to all streams.

 Unfortunately, repealing the rule using the Congressional Review Act would effectively prevent any and all new rules to protect streams from mountaintop mining. This could impair the work of the agencies to regulate the impacts of coal on watersheds.
